newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan, Iran to combine Afghan peace moves.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan, Iran to combine Afghan peace moves.

text.p: Pakistan and Iran agreed in talks on Thursday to jointly strive for peace in neighbouring war-torn Afghanistan, Pakistani officials said.

The talks followed the arrival of Iranian deputy foreign minister Alaeddin Boroujerdi for a day's visit amid hectic diplomatic activity to persuade Afghanistan's dominant Taleban Islamic movement and its opponents to stop fighting.

"It was emphasised that Iran and Pakistan would use their influence to induce the (opposition) northern alliance and the Taleban leadership to sit together for a peaceful solution of the Afghan problem," a Pakistan government statement said.

Differences between Pakistan and Iran on the Afghan conflict widened after Islamabad recognised the Taleban government in May while Iran continued its recognition of ousted president Burhanuddin Rabbani.
But a Pakistani Foreign Ministry spokesman told reporters on Thursday that Islamabad and Tehran should coordinate their peace moves.
"Both sides agreed (in Thursday's talks) that the solution to the Afghan problem lay in various Afghan factions sitting together and working out a peaceful settlement," the Pakistani statement said.
"Both sides also reiterated their vested interest for peace in Afghanistan as both countries were directly affected by the turmoil in Afghanistan," it said.
In Afghanistan, the official Kabul radio said Taleban forces repulsed two opposition attacks on Thursday in Bangi district of the northeastern province of Takhar.
Pakistan has offered to host intra-Afghan peace talks with the participation of Afghanistan's immediate neighbours as well as the United States and Russia.
The Pakistani spokesman said Islamabad would welcome Rabbani as a faction leader rather than Afghan president.
Commenting on reports that Rabbani's government, ousted from Kabul last September, has declared the northern town of Mazar-i-Sharif as its temporary capital, the spokesman said:
"All I can say is that we do not recognise this government. We have made our position very clear on this."
He said Pakistan, whose officials have held talks with the Taleban and opposition factions in Afghanistan in recent weeks, had no peace policy separate from that of the United Nations.
"Whatever we do, we are trying to supplement the U.N. efforts," he said.

The opposition wants demilitarisation of Kabul and formation of a political commission to chart outlines of a broad-based government. Taleban refuses to demilitarise Kabul and wants a ceasefire and release of its prisoners before peace talks.

Pakistan recognised the Taleban government in late May after the militia briefly captured Mazar-i-Sharif with the help of opposition leader General Abdul Malik. Recognition then came from Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.
Malik turned on the Taleban at the end of May, linking up with a Shi'ite Moslem Hezb-i-Wahdat faction to drive them from Mazar-i-Sharif after 15 hours of street fighting.
